papers.title: Fluctuation, correlation and perturbation-response behavior of nature-made and artificial nanobodies
Fluctuation, correlation and perturbation-response behavior of nature-made and artificial nanobodies
Artificial life as controlled disequilibrium
papers.abstract: Artificial Life can be modeled using simulated au-topoiesis. Liquid Automata are used to define simulated chemical reaction systems; particle systems with rules governing how particles are transformed on collision with each other. Unlike cellular automata, there is no fixed grid or time-step, only particles moving about and colliding in continuous space/time. These systems may give rise to emergent artificial life, or they may be (artificially) lifeless. Can we distinguish between these systems by analysing their equilibria?
papers.categories: Artificial life; Disequilibrium; Cellular automaton; Computer science; Artificial intelligence

papers.title: Perspectives for Strong Artificial Life
papers.abstract: This chapter introduces the twin deadlocks of strong artificial life. Conceptualization of life is a deadlock both because of the existence of a continuum between the inert and the living, and because we only know one instance of life. Computationalism is a second deadlock since it remains a matter of faith. Nevertheless, artificial life realizations quickly progress and recent constructions embed an always-growing set of the intuitive properties of life. This growing gap between theory and realizations should sooner or later crystallize in some kind of “paradigm shift” and then give clues to break the twin deadlocks.Request access from your librarian to read this chapter's full text.

papers.title: Towards origins of virtual artificial life: an overview
papers.abstract: The field of artificial life (ALife) studies 'life as it could be', in contrast to biology's study of 'life as we know it to be'. This includes a wide range of potential physical substrates, from synthetic biology (new genes), through xenobiology (new amino acids and DNA bases), inorganic chemistry (different structural elements), soft and hard robotics (new kinds of bodies) and also virtual life (existing inside a computer). Since any such life forms are artificial, the originating mechanisms can be similarly artificial, or can attempt to emulate natural mechanisms. Given the wide range of possible substrates and origins, it is crucial to have good definitions, and well-defined ways to detect and measure life, if and when it originates. This overview examines the current state of the art in ALife in defining, detecting and originating its subject matter, with its main focus on virtual life. After discussing common properties of several definitions of life, the overview synthesizes an engineering-focussed definition, in terms of abstract requirements, generic designs and specific implementation mechanisms, and then reviews the current state of the art through this lens. Although virtual ALife that satisfies all these requirements is yet to be exhibited, significant progress has been made on engineering individual mechanisms and, arguably, partially alive systems.This article is part of the theme issue 'Origins of life: the possible and the actual'.
papers.categories: Artificial life; Computer science; Theme (computing); Artificial intelligence; Field (mathematics)

papers.title: Substrate-Coupled Artificial Life: From Virtual Origins to Physical Silicon
papers.abstract: Artificial life studies life-like organisation across possible substrates, and classifies its bottom-up systems by where the artificial organism appears: in a physico-chemical, physico-mechanical, or computational medium. We argue that this taxonomy leaves a second axis underspecified, the causal role of the computing substrate itself, and that the omission carries a cost. The stakes of this missing axis are visible in the field’s recent stocktaking: virtual artificial life has not yet exhibited a system that satisfies the full requirements of life (autopoiesis, agency, and open-ended adaptation), with thermodynamic abstraction and the brittleness of symbolic substrates recurring as limitations (Stepney, 2025). We propose substrate-coupled artificial life (SCAL) as a research programme in which the physical dynamics of the substrate participate causally in the production, persistence, and adaptation of life-like organisation, rather than serving as an inert execution layer. The framework is grounded in three observations about conventional silicon: 1/f noise from charge-trap dynamics at MOSFET interfaces, a cache-hierarchy latency gradient that satisfies Lewontin-style criteria for differential persistence among self-reinforcing memory-topology structures, and DRAM operating far from equilibrium as a Prigogine-class dissipative structure. We specify the experimental requirements such a programme implies in conventional silicon and set out specific falsification criteria. The work is theoretical and pre-experimental: it defines the framework, identifies the experimental commitments required to test it, and specifies the conditions under which it would fail.
papers.categories: Artificial life; Dissipative system; Abstraction; Computer science; Adaptation (eye)

papers.title: An Auditable Complexity Ladder for Mechanism-Level Experiments in Artificial Life
papers.abstract: Open-ended evolution (OEE) research lacks standard exemplars and agreed metrics (Bedau, 2024). We do not claim to have achieved OEE. We contribute a methodological result: a protocol that makes mechanism-level claims in artificial life auditable, and a worked eleven-level exemplar (C0–C10) in a minimal-cell model (Parcells) that puts it under load. The protocol rests on four pillars. (i) Prospective freeze criteria and a two-gate admission decision. Each level adds one mechanistic capability or controlled configuration change; its numeric gates are frozen before the confirmatory sweep that judges them, and admission requires passing both a machine-checked per-run gate with REFUTE controls and an analyst-computed, human-adjudicated advantage contrast. We report which gate is machine-enforced and which is not, and audit per level which controls actually executed (Table 1). (ii) Failure retention. Negative results and our own confounded analyses are disclosed rather than buried — including one instance where an initial C10 sweep reused a single control across all stress magnitudes, producing a “stress window” that a paired 900-run factorial retest showed does not exist below the threshold originally claimed. (iii) Byte-safe RNG isolation , which makes “disabling a level changes nothing downstream” a byte-for-byte guarantee rather than an assertion. (iv) Evidence identity and grade , with every frozen verdict carrying an artifact↔code identity chain and an explicit evidence_grade — and with the known defects in that chain reported, including one over-broad identity hash that fails on drift it should ignore. Two boundaries are load-bearing: several freeze criteria could not have failed under the randomization they were re-run against, and the ladder demonstrates the discipline rather than establishing that all eleven levels are equally strong. A clean-checkout reproducible bundle accompanies this manuscript.
papers.categories: Identity (music); Computer science; Protocol (science); Construct (python library); Audit

papers.title: Substrate-Coupled Artificial Life: From Virtual Origins to Physical Silicon
papers.abstract: Artificial life studies life-like organisation across substrates. The standard bottom-up taxonomy distinguishes physico-chemical, physico-mechanical, and computational substrates (Stepney, 2025), and classifies where an artificial organism appears. A recent overview of virtual artificial life (Stepney, 2025) concludes that virtual systems satisfying the full requirements of life (autopoiesis, agency, and open-ended adaptation) have not yet been exhibited, and identifies thermodynamic abstraction and the brittleness of symbolic substrates as recurrent limitations. We argue that an axis orthogonal to the standard taxonomy has remained underspecified: the causal role of the computing substrate itself. We propose substrate-coupled artificial life (SCAL) as a research programme in which the physical dynamics of the substrate participate causally in the production, persistence, and adaptation of life-like organisation, rather than serving as an inert execution layer. The framework is grounded in three observations about conventional silicon: 1/f noise from charge-trap dynamics at MOSFET interfaces, a cache-hierarchy latency gradient that satisfies Lewontin-style criteria for differential persistence among self-reinforcing memory-topology structures, and DRAM operating far from equilibrium as a Prigogine-class dissipative structure. We specify the experimental requirements such a programme implies in conventional silicon and set out specific falsification criteria. papers.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
papers.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

papers.title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Vacuum Bubbles
papers.authors: Miguel Barroso Varela; Katherine Freese; Matthew Kleban; Cameron Norton; Evangelos I. Sfakianakis
papers.abstract: Quantum tunneling transverse to the inflaton trajectory can produce $10^6$--$10^8M_\odot$ primordial black holes at the abundance of JWST's little red dots, without the enhanced curvature perturbations excluded by limits on CMB spectral distortions. Rare vacuum bubbles nucleate during a brief interval of inflation and later form black holes, with adjustable mass and abundance and a narrow mass spectrum of percent-level width. The leading constraint, from accretion, is satisfied for a population matching the bright little red dots even if all the emitted radiation escapes as hard X-rays.

papers.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
papers.authors: Yuxin Jiang; Wenqiang Sun; Jiaqi Li; Yuchao Gu; Lvmin Zhang; Ivor Tsang; Mike Zheng Shou
papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

papers.title: Fractional Charge at Dislocations from Band-Inversion Cancellation
papers.abstract: Band inversions with opposite Chern numbers cancel in the Hall response and yield counterpropagating boundary modes that can gap out. However, a bulk probe of the topology that survives such a cancellation is lacking. We here show that dislocations in inversion-symmetric two-band crystals with cancelling band inversions bind a half-integer charge, which reveals the quantized bulk polarization of the bond-centered obstructed atomic limit realized by such crystals. To demonstrate this, we continuously deform a broad class of two-band lattice models into decoupled chains, without closing the bulk gap or breaking the inversion symmetry, where the dislocation charge follows from a count of occupied bonds. Notably, the fractional part of this charge is insensitive to local perturbations of the dislocation core, and it therefore persists after the in-gap core state is removed, as we show analytically in the chain limit and numerically away from it. In the Weyl-semimetal counterpart, the response to a magnetic flux separates this crystalline charge from the charge set by the Chern number of each momentum slice. We propose that a half-integer core charge that persists after the in-gap peak disappears from the local spectrum can be detected in artificial electronic and optical lattices, with metamaterials providing complementary access to the core modes.

papers.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
papers.authors: Amine Lbath; Manan Suri; Aurelien Delaitre; Vadim Okun; Massih-Reza Amini; Dinesh Manocha
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

papers.title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
papers.authors: Yang Meng; Zixin Ding; Robert L. Grossman; Yuxin Chen
papers.abstract: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

papers.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Kai Lu; Chenyang Ma; Ioannis Havoutis
papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

papers.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
papers.authors: Terence D. Agbeyegbe; Toneukarin G. Agbeyegbe
papers.abstract: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.
